```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

A nonlinear system asks for values of the unknowns `u` that make a residual
vanish: `f(u, p) = 0`. ModelingToolkit.jl builds such problems from
symbolic equations and hands them to NonlinearSolve.jl; modelcompR ports both
layers to R. This article covers the problem types (nonlinear, least
squares, interval, steady state, strongly connected component, homotopy and
linear problems), the solver catalog of NonlinearSolve, the solver options
and the fields of a solution.

```{r setup}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(modelcompR))
```

Every algorithm in this article is a constructor named as in Julia, and every
problem is solved by `solve(prob, alg, ...)`. A small helper prints the
outcome of several algorithms on one problem side by side; the names of
the list label the rows, and the `alg` column shows the method that
produced the result (for a polyalgorithm, the stage that won).

```{r}
compare <- function(prob, algs, ...) {
  rows <- lapply(algs, function(alg) {
    sol <- solve(prob, alg, ...)
    data.frame(alg = if (is.null(sol$stats$alg)) alg$name else sol$stats$alg,
               retcode = sol$retcode, u = paste(signif(unname(sol$u), 8), collapse = ", "),
               steps = sol$stats$nsteps, resid = signif(max(abs(sol$resid)), 2))
  })
  out <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  if (!is.null(names(algs))) rownames(out) <- names(algs)
  out
}
```

## Nonlinear systems from equations

A system without an independent variable is a nonlinear system. Equations
are written as R formulas with `0` on the left, as in Julia's
`0 ~ x^2 + y^2 - a`. Here the unknowns are the intersection of a circle of
radius `sqrt(a)` and the diagonal.

```{r}
cx <- Variable("cx"); cy <- Variable("cy"); ca <- Parameter("ca")
circ <- complete(System(list(0 ~ cx^2 + cy^2 - ca, 0 ~ cx - cy), name = "circ"))
circ
```

`complete()` marks the system as finished, the counterpart of `complete(sys)`
in ModelingToolkit. `NonlinearProblem(sys, op)` takes an operating point: a
list of initial guesses for the unknowns and values for the parameters.

```{r}
cprob <- NonlinearProblem(circ, list(cx ~ 1, cy ~ 2, ca ~ 2))
cprob
csol <- solve(cprob)
csol
```

### Solution fields

A `NonlinearSolution` holds the solution `u`, the residual `resid` at `u`,
the return code, the problem, the algorithm and statistics. Symbolic indexing
works as for time series solutions: any expression of the unknowns and
parameters can be evaluated at the solution.

```{r}
names(csol)
csol$retcode
successful_retcode(csol)
csol$resid
csol$stats
csol[cx]
csol[cx + 2 * cy]
csol$ps[ca]
```

The return codes follow SciMLBase: `"Success"`, `"StalledSuccess"`,
`"Stalled"`, `"MaxIters"`, `"Unstable"`, `"InitialFailure"`,
`"ConvergenceFailure"` and so on; `successful_retcode()` tells whether a code
counts as converged.

### Changing parameters and guesses

`remake()` rebuilds a problem with new parameter values or guesses without
regenerating code. With `ca = 8` the root moves to `(2, 2)`.

```{r}
solve(remake(cprob, p = list(ca ~ 8)))$u
```

Unknowns without a value in the operating point start from the `guess`
metadata of the variable or from the `guesses` of the system, which may be
expressions of other unknowns and parameters.

```{r}
gx <- Variable("gx", guess = 3); gy <- Variable("gy")
gsys <- complete(System(list(0 ~ gx^2 - 4, 0 ~ gy - gx), name = "gsys",
                        guesses = list(gy ~ 2 * gx)))
gprob <- NonlinearProblem(gsys, list())
gprob$u0
solve(gprob)$u
```

When neither is available the constructor stops with an error; the argument
`missing_guess_value = MissingGuessValue$Constant(1)` fills the gaps with a
constant instead.

### The generated function and Jacobian

`NonlinearFunction(sys, jac = TRUE)` returns the generated residual
`f(u, p)` and its symbolic Jacobian; `NonlinearProblem()` generates the
Jacobian by default, so Newton type methods do not need finite differences.

```{r}
cfun <- NonlinearFunction(circ, jac = TRUE)
cfun$f(c(1, 2), 2)
cfun$jac(c(1, 2), 2)
```

## Tearing with `mtkcompile()`

`mtkcompile()` runs the structural pipeline of ModelingToolkit: alias
elimination, matching, and tearing, which solves as many equations as
possible explicitly and keeps the solved variables as observed equations. In
the current port the full pipeline runs for systems with an independent
variable, so the way to tear an algebraic system is to declare the unknowns
as functions of `t` and write only algebraic equations. A
`NonlinearProblem` built from a time dependent system sets every derivative
to zero.

```{r}
t <- t_nounits
variables("tx(t)", "ty(t)", "tz(t)")
parameters("ta", "tb")
teqs <- list(0 ~ tx + ty - ta, 0 ~ ty^3 + ty - tz, 0 ~ tz - 2 * tx + tb)
torn <- mtkcompile(System(teqs, t, name = "torn"))
torn
observed(torn)
```

Three equations became one: `tx` and `tz` are computed from `ty`, and the
solver iterates on `ty` alone. The observed variables are still available
from the solution.

```{r}
tsol <- solve(NonlinearProblem(torn, list(ty ~ 1, ta ~ 3, tb ~ 1)))
tsol$u
c(tx = tsol[tx], ty = tsol[ty], tz = tsol[tz])
```

The same equations in a `System` without `t` are solved as a coupled system
of three unknowns; `mtkcompile()` returns them unchanged.

## Problems from R functions

`NonlinearProblem`, `NonlinearLeastSquaresProblem`,
`IntervalNonlinearProblem` and `SteadyStateProblem` also accept a plain R
function, the counterpart of `NonlinearProblem(f, u0, p)` in Julia. The
residual has the signature `f(u, p)` (`f(u, p, t)` for steady states).

```{r}
solve(NonlinearProblem(function(u, p) u^2 - p, 1, 2))$u
```

`NonlinearFunction(f, jac = J)` attaches an analytic Jacobian; without it
the solvers use finite differences. The Rosenbrock residuals from Powell's
badly scaled start make a standard test problem.

```{r}
rosen <- function(u, p) c(10 * (u[2] - u[1]^2), 1 - u[1])
rosen_jac <- function(u, p) rbind(c(-20 * u[1], 10), c(-1, 0))
rprob <- NonlinearProblem(NonlinearFunction(rosen, jac = rosen_jac), c(-1.2, 1))
solve(rprob, NewtonRaphson())$u
```

## The default algorithm and polyalgorithms

Without an algorithm, `solve()` uses a polyalgorithm, as NonlinearSolve
does. A polyalgorithm tries a list of methods in turn, each from the initial
guess, and returns the first success. `FastShortcutNonlinearPolyalg()` holds
Broyden, Klement, Newton, two trust region variants and Levenberg Marquardt;
for problems with at most 25 unknowns it starts at Newton, and when the
problem has a Jacobian function it leaves out the quasi Newton methods. The
winning method is recorded in `sol$stats$alg`.

```{r}
vapply(FastShortcutNonlinearPolyalg()$algs, function(a) a$name, "")
FastShortcutNonlinearPolyalg(u0_len = 10)$start_index
solve(rprob)$stats$alg
```

`RobustMultiNewton()` tries trust region methods with several radius updates
and Newton with and without a line search; `FastShortcutNLLSPolyalg()` is the
default for least squares problems. Any list of algorithms can be combined
with `NonlinearSolvePolyAlgorithm()`.

```{r}
compare(rprob, list(robust = RobustMultiNewton(),
                    custom = NonlinearSolvePolyAlgorithm(list(Broyden(), TrustRegion()))))
```

The order matters. For `u^3 - 8` from `u = 0` the Jacobian vanishes at the
start, so Newton's method and the trust region methods cannot move, and the
default (which starts at Newton for small problems) fails, exactly as in
Julia. The quasi Newton methods start from a scaled identity Jacobian and
succeed, and so does the polyalgorithm when it starts at Broyden.

```{r}
cube <- NonlinearProblem(function(u, p) u^3 - p, 0, 8)
solve(cube)$retcode
compare(cube, list(broyden = Broyden(), klement = Klement(),
                   polyalg_from_broyden = FastShortcutNonlinearPolyalg()))
```

## The solver catalog

### Newton type methods

`NewtonRaphson()` is Newton's method, optionally with a backtracking line
search. `TrustRegion()` is NonlinearSolve's trust region method: More's
nearly exact subproblem (the `lmpar` step of MINPACK) with the radius update
selected by `radius_update_scheme`. `LevenbergMarquardt()` adds damping to
the Gauss Newton step and `GaussNewton()` is the undamped least squares
method; both also solve square systems.

```{r}
compare(rprob, list(newton = NewtonRaphson(),
                    newton_backtracking = NewtonRaphson(linesearch = "BackTracking"),
                    trustregion = TrustRegion(), lm = LevenbergMarquardt(),
                    gaussnewton = GaussNewton()))
```

`PseudoTransient()` is pseudo transient continuation: a Newton step damped by
the inverse of a pseudo time step `alpha`, which grows by the switched
evolution relaxation rule as the residual falls. A small `alpha_initial`
(the default is `1e-3`) takes many short, safe steps; a large one behaves
like Newton's method.

```{r}
cube05 <- NonlinearProblem(function(u, p) u^3 - 8, 0.5)
compare(cube05, list(ptc_default = PseudoTransient(), ptc_alpha1 = PseudoTransient(alpha_initial = 1),
                     newton = NewtonRaphson()))
```

### Trust region radius updates

`RadiusUpdateSchemes` lists the update rules of NonlinearSolve. `"More"` is
the default with More's subproblem and `"Simple"` with the dogleg
subproblem (`TrustRegion(subproblem = TrustRegionSubproblem$Dogleg)` or
`TrustRegionDogleg()`).

```{r}
unlist(RadiusUpdateSchemes)
schemes <- c("Simple", "NLsolve", "NocedalWright", "Hei", "Yuan", "Bastin", "Fan")
compare(rprob, sapply(schemes, function(s) TrustRegion(radius_update_scheme = s),
                      simplify = FALSE))
```

The thresholds and factors of the radius update are arguments of
`TrustRegion()` (`step_threshold`, `shrink_threshold`, `expand_threshold`,
`shrink_factor`, `expand_factor`, `initial_trust_radius`,
`max_trust_radius`).

### Quasi Newton and spectral methods

Quasi Newton methods evaluate the Jacobian at most once, at the start. `Broyden()`
updates an approximate inverse Jacobian with the good or bad Broyden rule;
`Klement()` keeps a diagonal approximation; `LimitedMemoryBroyden()` stores
only a few update vectors. `DFSane()` is the derivative free spectral method
with a nonmonotone line search. The examples in the next sections use the
circle problem again, written as an R function and started from `(2, 0.5)`.

```{r}
qprob <- NonlinearProblem(function(u, p) c(u[1]^2 + u[2]^2 - 2, u[1] - u[2]), c(2, 0.5))
compare(qprob, list(good_broyden = Broyden(), bad_broyden = Broyden(update_rule = "bad_broyden"),
                    broyden_true_jac = Broyden(init_jacobian = "true_jacobian"),
                    klement_true_jac = Klement(init_jacobian = "true_jacobian"),
                    lbroyden = LimitedMemoryBroyden(), dfsane = DFSane()))
```

### SimpleNonlinearSolve

The light methods of SimpleNonlinearSolve are available under their Julia
names: `SimpleNewtonRaphson()`, `SimpleTrustRegion()`, `SimpleBroyden()`,
`SimpleKlement()`, `SimpleDFSane()`, `SimpleLimitedMemoryBroyden()`,
`SimpleGaussNewton()` and the third order `SimpleHalley()`.

```{r}
compare(qprob, list(SimpleNewtonRaphson(), SimpleTrustRegion(), SimpleBroyden(),
                    SimpleKlement(), SimpleDFSane(), SimpleHalley()))
```

### Composing a method

The methods above are instances of `GeneralizedFirstOrderAlgorithm()`, which
combines a descent direction (`NewtonDescent()`, `DampedNewtonDescent()`,
`SteepestDescent()`, `Dogleg()`, `MoreTrustRegionDescent()`,
`GeodesicAcceleration()`) with a globalization: a line search or a
`GenericTrustRegionScheme()`.

```{r}
compare(qprob, list(
  damped_newton = GeneralizedFirstOrderAlgorithm(descent = DampedNewtonDescent()),
  geodesic = GeneralizedFirstOrderAlgorithm(descent = GeodesicAcceleration()),
  steepest_backtracking = GeneralizedFirstOrderAlgorithm(descent = SteepestDescent(),
                                                         linesearch = BackTracking()),
  dogleg_hei = GeneralizedFirstOrderAlgorithm(descent = Dogleg(),
                                              trustregion = GenericTrustRegionScheme("Hei"))))
```

### Line searches

The line searches of LineSearch.jl and LineSearches.jl are ported:
`BackTracking()`, `ArmijoLineSearch()`, `GoldenSection()`,
`LiFukushimaLineSearch()`, `StrongWolfeLineSearch()`,
`MoreThuenteLineSearch()`, `HagerZhangLineSearch()`,
`RobustNonMonotoneLineSearch()`, `ProjectedBackTracking()` and
`NoLineSearch()`, plus `LineSearchesJL()` naming a LineSearches.jl method.

```{r}
searches <- list(none = NoLineSearch(), backtracking = BackTracking(),
                 backtracking2 = BackTracking(order = 2), armijo = ArmijoLineSearch(),
                 lifukushima = LiFukushimaLineSearch(), strongwolfe = StrongWolfeLineSearch(),
                 hagerzhang = HagerZhangLineSearch(), linesearchesjl = LineSearchesJL("HagerZhang"))
compare(rprob, lapply(searches, function(ls) GeneralizedFirstOrderAlgorithm(linesearch = ls)))
```

On this problem the full Newton step happens to reach the root in two steps;
a line search shortens the first steps, which costs iterations here but is
what keeps Newton's method from diverging from poor starting points.

## Solver options

Options go to `solve()`: `abstol` (tolerance on the residual, default
`eps^0.8`), `reltol`, `maxiters` (default 1000) and `termination_condition`.
A loose tolerance stops early with a larger residual; a tiny iteration
budget returns `"MaxIters"`.

```{r}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1e-2, 1e-6, 1e-12), function(tol)
  cbind(abstol = tol, compare(cube05, list(Broyden()), abstol = tol))))
compare(rprob, list(LevenbergMarquardt()), maxiters = 3)
```

The termination modes of NonlinearSolve decide when a solve stops.
`AbsTerminationMode()` tests every residual component against `abstol`, the
`Norm` modes test a norm, and the safe modes also stop with `"Unstable"` when
the residual blows up or `"Stalled"` when it stops improving. The safe best
variants return the best iterate seen; the default is
`AbsNormSafeBestTerminationMode(max_stalled_steps = 32)`.

```{r}
modes <- list(AbsTerminationMode(), RelTerminationMode(), NormTerminationMode(),
              AbsNormTerminationMode(), RelNormSafeTerminationMode(),
              AbsNormSafeBestTerminationMode())
vapply(modes, function(tm)
  solve(qprob, NewtonRaphson(), termination_condition = tm)$retcode, "")
```

Jacobians come from the problem when it has one (the symbolic Jacobian of a
system, or the `jac` of a `NonlinearFunction`), and otherwise from finite
differences. The `autodiff` arguments of the Julia signatures accept the
ADTypes of the package, such as `AutoFiniteDiff()` and `AutoForwardDiff()`;
with `AutoFiniteDiff()` the bounded solvers use the bound aware finite
differences of NonlinearSolve, which never step outside the box.

```{r}
solve(NonlinearProblem(rosen, c(-1.2, 1)), TrustRegion(autodiff = AutoFiniteDiff()))$u
solve(NonlinearProblem(rosen, c(-1.2, 1)), TrustRegion(autodiff = AutoForwardDiff()))$u
```

## Nonlinear least squares

`NonlinearLeastSquaresProblem` minimizes the sum of squared residuals when
there are more residuals than unknowns, or when no exact root exists. The
residuals `(u1 - 1, u1 + 1, u2 - 3)` cannot all vanish; the minimizer is
`(0, 3)` with residual `(-1, 1, 0)`.

```{r}
lsq <- NonlinearLeastSquaresProblem(function(u, p) c(u[1] - 1, u[1] + 1, u[2] - 3), c(5, 5))
compare(lsq, list(GaussNewton(), LevenbergMarquardt(), FastShortcutNLLSPolyalg()))
solve(lsq)$resid
```

From a symbolic system with more equations than unknowns the problem is
built the same way.

```{r}
lx <- Variable("lx"); ly <- Variable("ly")
lsys <- complete(System(list(0 ~ lx + ly - 3, 0 ~ lx - ly - 1, 0 ~ 2 * lx - 4), name = "lsys"))
solve(NonlinearLeastSquaresProblem(lsys, list(lx ~ 0, ly ~ 0)))$u
```

A curve fit is a least squares problem in the parameters of the model. Here
an exponential `a exp(b t)` is fitted to six points.

```{r}
tt <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5); yy <- c(1, 1.6, 2.8, 4.4, 7.6, 12)
fit <- NonlinearLeastSquaresProblem(
  NonlinearFunction(function(u, p) u[1] * exp(u[2] * tt) - yy, resid_prototype = numeric(6)),
  c(1, 0.5))
fsol <- solve(fit, LevenbergMarquardt())
fsol$u
sum(fsol$resid^2)
```

## Bounds and bounded solvers

Bounds `lb <= u <= ub` come from the `bounds` metadata of the variables or
from the `lb` and `ub` arguments. Algorithms without native bounds run on the
smooth transformation of `bounds_transform.jl`; the bounded solvers of
NonlinearSolveFirstOrder handle the box directly.

```{r}
bx <- Variable("bx", bounds = c(-10, 0))
bprob <- NonlinearProblem(complete(System(list(0 ~ bx^2 - 4), name = "bsys")), list(bx ~ -0.1))
c(bprob$lb, bprob$ub)
solve(bprob, TrustRegion())$u
```

The bounded methods are `TrustRegionReflective()` (Coleman and Li),
`Dogbox()`, `BoundedLevenbergMarquardt()`, `BoundedGaussNewton()` with a line
search or trust region globalization, and `BoundedTrustRegion()`. Their
statistics count residual and Jacobian evaluations, factorizations and
linear solves.

```{r}
rbox <- NonlinearProblem(NonlinearFunction(rosen, jac = rosen_jac), u0 = c(-1.2, 1),
                         lb = c(-2, -2), ub = c(2, 2))
balgs <- list(TrustRegionReflective(), Dogbox(), BoundedLevenbergMarquardt(),
              BoundedGaussNewton(), BoundedGaussNewton(globalization = "trustregion"),
              BoundedTrustRegion())
do.call(rbind, lapply(balgs, function(alg) {
  s <- solve(rbox, alg)
  data.frame(alg = alg$name, retcode = s$retcode, u1 = s$u[1], u2 = s$u[2],
             nf = s$stats$nf, njacs = s$stats$njacs, nsteps = s$stats$nsteps)
}))
```

When the root lies outside the box the bounded solvers stop at the
constrained stationary point with `"Stalled"`. With `ub = (0.5, 2)` the
Rosenbrock root `(1, 1)` is excluded. The options `store_trace = TRUE` and
`trace_level = TraceMinimal()` (or `TraceWithJacobianConditionNumber()`,
`TraceAll()`) keep one entry per step in `sol$trace`; `show_trace = TRUE`
prints them as the solve runs.

```{r}
rcut <- remake(rbox, ub = c(0.5, 2))
s <- solve(rcut, Dogbox(), store_trace = TRUE, trace_level = TraceMinimal())
s$retcode
s$u
do.call(rbind, lapply(s$trace$history, function(e)
  data.frame(iteration = e$iteration, fnorm = e$fnorm, stepnorm = e$stepnorm)))
```

The default for a problem with bounds is
`SobolMultistart(FastShortcutBoundedPolyalg())`, which restarts the bounded
polyalgorithm from Sobol points in the box until one start succeeds.

```{r}
solve(rbox)$u
solve(rbox, SobolMultistart(nstarts = 4))$retcode
```

## Wrapped solvers

NonlinearSolve wraps solvers from other Julia packages; modelcompR
implements each natively after the original: `NLsolveJL()` (trust region,
Newton, Anderson and Broyden), `CMINPACK()` (Powell's hybrid method and More's
Levenberg Marquardt), `SIAMFANLEquationsJL()` (Newton, pseudo transient,
secant and Anderson), `FixedPointAccelerationJL()` and `SpeedMappingJL()`
(fixed point accelerations of the map `u + f(u)`), `LeastSquaresOptimJL()`,
`FastLevenbergMarquardtJL()`, `NLSolversJL()` and `PETScSNES()`.

```{r}
circ2 <- NonlinearProblem(function(u, p) c(u[1]^2 + u[2]^2 - 4, u[1] * u[2] - 1), c(2, 0.5))
compare(circ2, list(nlsolve_tr = NLsolveJL(), nlsolve_newton = NLsolveJL(method = "newton"),
                    nlsolve_anderson = NLsolveJL(method = "anderson"), cminpack = CMINPACK(),
                    siam_newton = SIAMFANLEquationsJL(), lso_dogleg = LeastSquaresOptimJL("dogleg"),
                    fastlm = FastLevenbergMarquardtJL(), nlsolvers = NLSolversJL(),
                    petsc = PETScSNES()))
```

Fixed point methods need the map `u + f(u)` to be a contraction near the
root. The system `u = (0.5 cos(u2) + 0.1, 0.5 sin(u1) + 0.2)` is one, and
every acceleration converges.

```{r}
fixp <- NonlinearProblem(function(u, p) c(0.5 * cos(u[2]) - u[1] + 0.1,
                                          0.5 * sin(u[1]) - u[2] + 0.2), c(0, 0))
compare(fixp, list(fpa_anderson = FixedPointAccelerationJL(),
                   fpa_mpe = FixedPointAccelerationJL(algorithm = "MPE"),
                   fpa_aitken = FixedPointAccelerationJL(algorithm = "Aitken"),
                   speedmapping = SpeedMappingJL(),
                   siam_anderson = SIAMFANLEquationsJL(method = "anderson", m = 2)))
```

A step count of `-1` (or `0` for SIAMFANLEquations) means the wrapped package
does not report that count. As in MINPACK.jl, `CMINPACK()` records its call
counts only with `store_trace = TRUE`.

```{r}
unlist(solve(circ2, CMINPACK(), store_trace = TRUE)$stats[c("nf", "njacs")])
```

## Interval problems and bracketing

A scalar equation with a sign change over an interval is an
`IntervalNonlinearProblem`. Bracketing methods keep the root enclosed and
always converge. `ITP()` (interpolate, truncate and project) is the default;
`Bisection()`, `Brent()`, `Falsi()`, `Ridder()`, `Muller()`, `Alefeld()` and
`ModAB()` are the alternatives.

```{r}
ix <- Variable("ix"); ia <- Parameter("ia")
iprob <- IntervalNonlinearProblem(complete(System(list(0 ~ ix^2 - ia), name = "isys")),
                                  c(0, 3), list(ia ~ 2))
isol <- solve(iprob)
isol$alg$name
isol[ix]
c(isol$left, isol$right)
```

```{r}
dottie <- IntervalNonlinearProblem(function(u, p) cos(u) - u, c(0, 1))
do.call(rbind, lapply(list(ITP(), Bisection(), Brent(), Falsi(), Ridder(), Muller(),
                           Alefeld(), ModAB()), function(alg) {
  s <- solve(dottie, alg, abstol = 1e-12)
  data.frame(alg = alg$name, retcode = s$retcode, u = sprintf("%.15f", s$u))
}))
```

A root at an end point is reported as `"ExactSolutionLeft"` or
`"ExactSolutionRight"`. An interval without a sign change fails with
`"InitialFailure"` and a warning.

```{r}
solve(IntervalNonlinearProblem(function(u, p) u - p, c(1, 2), p = 1))$retcode
bad <- solve(IntervalNonlinearProblem(function(u, p) u^2 + 1, c(0, 1)))
bad$retcode
```

## Steady states

A `SteadyStateProblem` asks for the equilibrium of an ODE system: the state
where every derivative vanishes. It is built from a compiled time dependent
system or from a function `f(u, p, t)`. Two algorithms solve it:
`SSRootfind()` solves `f(u, p, Inf) = 0` with a nonlinear solver, and
`DynamicSS()` integrates the ODE until the derivatives fall below its
tolerances.

```{r}
D <- D_nounits
dx <- Variable("dx", t); dk <- Parameter("dk"); ds <- Parameter("ds")
decay <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(dx) ~ ds - dk * dx), t, name = "decay"))
ssp <- SteadyStateProblem(decay, list(dx ~ 1, dk ~ 2, ds ~ 3))
solve(ssp, SSRootfind())
solve(ssp, SSRootfind(TrustRegion()))[dx]
solve(ssp, DynamicSS(abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-10)[dx]
```

The two approaches differ when the steady state is not unique. In a
reversible reaction `a <=> b` with rates 2 and 1 every point on the line
`b = 2 a` is a steady state. Integration from the initial state keeps the
total `a + b` and picks the point of the line with the initial total, which
a root finder alone cannot know.

```{r}
sa <- Variable("sa", t); sb <- Variable("sb", t)
revr <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(sa) ~ -2 * sa + sb, D(sb) ~ 2 * sa - sb), t, name = "rev"))
dd <- solve(SteadyStateProblem(revr, list(sa ~ 3, sb ~ 0)),
            DynamicSS(abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-10)
c(sa = dd[sa], sb = dd[sb])
```

From an R function, `DynamicSS()` picks a default ODE solver:

```{r}
solve(SteadyStateProblem(function(u, p, t) p[1] - p[2] * u, u0 = 0, p = c(3, 2)), DynamicSS())$u
```

## Strongly connected components

Large systems often decompose into blocks that can be solved one after
another. `SCCNonlinearProblem` matches equations to unknowns, finds the
strongly connected components of the dependency graph and solves them in
topological order: each block sees the values of the blocks before it. This
is ModelingToolkit's `SCCNonlinearProblem`, used for initialization of large
models.

```{r}
kx <- Variable("kx"); ky <- Variable("ky"); kz <- Variable("kz"); kw <- Variable("kw")
chain <- complete(System(list(0 ~ kz^2 + kz - ky, 0 ~ kx^3 - 8, 0 ~ ky - 2 * kx + kw,
                              0 ~ kw - ky + 4), name = "chain"))
scc <- SCCNonlinearProblem(chain, list(kx ~ 1, ky ~ 1, kz ~ 1, kw ~ 1))
lapply(scc$var_sccs, function(i) names(scc$u0)[i])
scc$scc_kinds
ssol <- solve(scc)
round(ssol$u, 10)
ssol$stats
```

`kx` is solved first, then the affine pair `(ky, kw)` in one linear step,
then `kz`. Blocks are classified as `"linear"`, `"nonlinear"` or
`"homotopy"` and each gets the matching treatment.

## Homotopy continuation

### The `homotopy()` operator

Newton's method converges only from a guess close enough to the root.
`homotopy(actual, simplified)` marks an expression with an easy surrogate,
as in Modelica: the solver starts with the surrogate and deforms it into the
actual expression, `lambda * actual + (1 - lambda) * simplified`, tracking
the root as `lambda` goes from 0 to 1. Numerically `homotopy()` evaluates
its first argument.

```{r}
hy <- Variable("hy")
hsys <- complete(System(list(0 ~ homotopy(atan(hy - 3), hy)), name = "hsys"))
homotopy_enabled(hsys)
plain <- solve(NonlinearProblem(hsys, list(hy ~ 12)), NewtonRaphson(), maxiters = 50)
plain$retcode
```

From `hy = 12` Newton's method on `atan(hy - 3)` overshoots and never settles on the root.
`HomotopyProblem` solves by continuation in `lambda`; the continuation
methods are `HomotopySweep()` (natural parameter continuation),
`KantorovichHomotopy()`, `ArcLengthContinuation()`, and the polyalgorithms
`HomotopyPolyAlgorithm()` and `FastShortcutHomotopyPolyalg()`.

```{r}
hprob <- HomotopyProblem(hsys, list(hy ~ 12))
do.call(rbind, lapply(list(HomotopySweep(), KantorovichHomotopy(), ArcLengthContinuation(),
                           HomotopyPolyAlgorithm()), function(alg) {
  s <- solve(hprob, alg)
  data.frame(alg = alg$name, retcode = s$retcode, hy = s[hy])
}))
```

`AbstractNonlinearProblem(sys, op)` returns a `HomotopyProblem` when the
system contains `homotopy()` nodes and a `NonlinearProblem` otherwise;
`strip_homotopy(sys)` replaces every node by its actual branch.

```{r}
class(AbstractNonlinearProblem(hsys, list(hy ~ 12)))[1]
equations(strip_homotopy(hsys))
```

### All roots of polynomial systems

For polynomial systems, `HomotopyContinuationProblem` finds every isolated
complex root by total degree homotopy, the method of HomotopyContinuation.jl:
it starts from a system with known roots, one path per root (the product of
the equation degrees), and tracks the paths in the complex plane. The solution
reports the root nearest the guess in `u` and all roots in `sol$original`.

```{r}
px <- Variable("px"); py <- Variable("py")
poly <- complete(System(list(0 ~ px^2 + py^2 - 5, 0 ~ px * py - 2), name = "poly"))
hcp <- HomotopyContinuationProblem(poly, list(px ~ 0.9, py ~ 2.2))
hcp$degrees
hsol <- solve(hcp, HomotopyContinuationJL())
hsol$u
hsol$original$n_paths
hsol$original$real_solutions
```

A system with no real root ends with `"ConvergenceFailure"`, while its complex
roots are still listed.

```{r}
none <- solve(HomotopyContinuationProblem(complete(System(list(0 ~ px^2 + 1), name = "none")),
                                          list(px ~ 0)))
none$retcode
none$original$solutions
```

## Linear problems

A system of affine equations becomes a `LinearProblem` `A u = b`.
ModelingToolkit extracts `A` and `b` symbolically; the constructor refuses
equations that are not affine in the unknowns.

```{r}
ux <- Variable("ux"); uy <- Variable("uy"); ua <- Parameter("ua")
lin <- complete(System(list(0 ~ 2 * ux + uy - ua, 0 ~ ux - uy), name = "lin"))
lprob <- LinearProblem(lin, list(ua ~ 3))
lprob$A
lprob$b
lsol <- solve(lprob)
lsol[ux]
solve(remake(lprob, p = list(ua ~ 6)))$u
```

### LinearSolve algorithms

The algorithms of LinearSolve.jl solve a `LinearProblem` built from a matrix
and a right hand side: dense factorizations (`LUFactorization()`,
`QRFactorization()`, `SVDFactorization()`, `CholeskyFactorization()`,
`LDLtFactorization()`, `BunchKaufmanFactorization()`, `KLUFactorization()`
and others) and Krylov methods (`KrylovJL_CG()`, `KrylovJL_GMRES()`,
`KrylovJL_BICGSTAB()`, `KrylovJL_MINRES()`, `KrylovJL_LSMR()` and others).

```{r}
A <- matrix(c(4, 1, 2, 1, 3, 0, 2, 0, 5), 3); b <- c(1, 2, 3)
mprob <- LinearProblem(A, b)
solve(A, b)
do.call(rbind, lapply(list(LUFactorization(), QRFactorization(), SVDFactorization(),
                           CholeskyFactorization(), KrylovJL_CG(), KrylovJL_GMRES()),
                      function(alg) {
  s <- solve(mprob, alg, reltol = 1e-12)
  data.frame(alg = alg$name, retcode = s$retcode, u = paste(signif(s$u, 8), collapse = ", "))
}))
```

Without an algorithm, `solve()` solves by QR. Passing `assumptions =
OperatorAssumptions()` lets the default of LinearSolve choose a
factorization from what is known about the operator: LU for square systems, QR for rectangular or ill conditioned
ones, SVD for severely ill conditioned ones. Rectangular systems get the
least squares solution.

```{r}
solve(mprob, assumptions = OperatorAssumptions(condition = OperatorCondition$SuperIllConditioned))$u
over <- LinearProblem(matrix(c(1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 2), 3), c(1, 2, 2))
solve(over, QRFactorization())$u
```

`init()` creates a `LinearCache` that keeps the factorization; replacing `b`
reuses it, as LinearSolve's caching interface does.

```{r}
cache <- init(LinearProblem(matrix(c(4, 1, 1, 3), 2), c(1, 2)), LUFactorization())
solve_integrator(cache)$u
cache$b <- c(2, 4)
solve_integrator(cache)$u
```

## Sensitivity of nonlinear solutions

The derivative of a root with respect to the parameters follows from the
implicit function theorem: `du/dp = -(df/du)^(-1) df/dp`. `solve_gradient()`
differentiates a scalar function of the solution, and
`adjoint_sensitivities()` with `SteadyStateAdjoint()` does the same for a
steady state. For `x^2 = a`, `dx/da = 1 / (2 sqrt(a))`.

```{r}
nx <- Variable("nx"); na <- Parameter("na")
nsys <- complete(System(list(0 ~ nx^2 - na), name = "nsys"))
solve_gradient(function(sol) sol$u[[1]], NonlinearProblem(nsys, list(nx ~ 1, na ~ 2)),
               NewtonRaphson())$p
1 / (2 * sqrt(2))
```

For the decay model, the steady state is `ds / dk`, so the gradient of
`x^2` is `(-2 ds^2 / dk^3, 2 ds / dk^2)`:

```{r}
r <- adjoint_sensitivities(solve(ssp, SSRootfind()), NULL, sensealg = SteadyStateAdjoint(),
                           g = function(u, p) u[1]^2)
r$dp
```

## Julia equivalents

| Julia | modelcompR |
|---|---|
| `@variables x y`, `@parameters a` | `Variable("x")`, `Parameter("a")` or `variables()`, `parameters()` |
| `NonlinearProblem(sys, [x => 1, a => 2])` | `NonlinearProblem(sys, list(x ~ 1, a ~ 2))` |
| `solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())` | `solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())` |
| `sol[x]`, `sol.ps[a]`, `sol.retcode` | `sol[x]`, `sol$ps[a]`, `sol$retcode` |
| `SciMLBase.successful_retcode(sol)` | `successful_retcode(sol)` |
| `IntervalNonlinearProblem(f, (0, 3), p)` | `IntervalNonlinearProblem(f, c(0, 3), p = p)` |
| `SteadyStateProblem(sys, u0p)` | `SteadyStateProblem(sys, op)` |
| `SCCNonlinearProblem(sys, op)` | `SCCNonlinearProblem(sys, op)` |
| `HomotopyContinuationProblem(sys, op)` | `HomotopyContinuationProblem(sys, op)` |
| `LinearProblem(A, b)`, `init(prob, alg)` | `LinearProblem(A, b)`, `init(prob, alg)` |
